To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a firm should offer an optional job rotation to an employee who is not only skilled but also versatile (and thus likely to have a high outside opportunity).

(a) a firm that wishes to match pay with skills should offer employees the opportunity to take on new tasks and (b) a firm can offer this opportunity in a manner that ensures that only a skilled employee wants it.

(1) a firm that wants to retain a skilled employee may offer the employee a chance to take on new tasks, and (2) the compensation arrangement for the new tasks should be structured so as to guarantee that the employee will only accept the new tasks if she is truly skilled.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of a compensation plan to induce employees to learn skills on the job that are valued by the firm, but not valued by employees in the external market.
the design of a job rotation program as a means for a firm to credibly signal to employees that the firm values on-the-job learning.
the design and implementation of an optional job rotation policy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a firm's job rotation programs are a valuable tool for assessing on-the-job learning.
job rotation programs are an excellent way to gauge on-the-job learning.
job rotation can be used as a tool to gauge an employee’s on-the-job learning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the firm's optimal compensation arrangement is to pay a fixed salary for a given job and then pay a bonus for the new tasks that the employee learns.
job rotation programs can serve as a mechanism for identifying skilled employees.
firms can use job rotation programs as a screening tool for identifying employees who have developed valuable skills on the job.

a firm's compensation structure can be designed to encourage employees to learn new skills.
